$comment: Guided walkthroughs rendered by the ontology browser. Each step may carry prose, a diagram (by filename in docs/diagrams/), terms to surface live, shapes whose constraint messages are quoted verbatim, and a table. `openQuestions` lists what remains undecided. Authored content — the terms and shapes referenced are resolved at build time and warned about if they do not exist.

explainers.title: Request path boundaries
explainers.subtitle: Platform entitlements at ingress, application authorization inside the boundary
explainers.summary: Coarse-grained platform authorization protects the right to enter an application and deployment boundary; resource authorization protects the right to perform an operation on an application resource. This walkthrough covers where that line sits, what sits on each side, and how the model stops the line from moving quietly.

steps.heading: The three layers
steps.body:
Coarse-grained platform authorization protects the right to enter an application and deployment boundary. Resource authorization protects the right to perform an operation on an application resource. Everything below follows from holding those two apart.

The symmetry is exact and worth reading twice: both are authorization, both have a subject, both end in a decision. What differs is the object being protected — a boundary in one case, a resource in the other — and that difference is what makes one platform-owned and the other application-owned. A boundary is the platform's to define because the platform put it there; a resource belongs to whoever built the application behind it.

One enforcement stack serves many independently developed applications, and that only works if the vocabulary ingress evaluates stays small and stable, and if nothing application-specific can enter it. The control plane defines entitlements; ingress enforces them; applications own everything past the boundary.

steps.heading: A request, resolved
steps.body:
Take a concrete request:

POST https://api.company.com/digital-bank/transactions/12345

Before any entitlement is evaluated, ingress resolves it to a platform endpoint. The route registry matches the domain and path, and everything the platform needs falls out of governed configuration — none of it asserted by the caller.

What ingress then knows is that a request is attempting to enter the digital bank's transactions boundary, in prod, in us-west-2. What it does not know, and never needs to, is that /12345 identifies an order. That is the line: the endpoint is registered platform configuration, the object behind it is application data.

With that resolved, the authorization request is the XACML tuple — subject Alice, action ACCESS, resource the application access endpoint — with the tenant, environment, region, channel, session and assurance as context. The decision point answers one question: may Alice, acting for this tenant, cross this boundary. Permit or Deny.

steps.heading: One request, three checkpoints
steps.body:
The three layers become three checkpoints on a single request, and the first distinction to make is between the first two — because it is the one people collapse.

Ingress is the enforcement point. It resolves and it enforces, but it does not decide: the domain and path give it the tenant, the application and the endpoint; the token gives it the principal; the cookie handle with its proof gives it the session; the journey definition gives it the channel and the assurance. None of that is a decision. It is the context a decision needs.

The platform PDP decides one thing — may this request cross into the application boundary — and answers Permit or Deny. Every check it makes is answerable with the application as an opaque identifier: membership, the five dimensions, enablement in scope, coverage, assurance. Nothing about what the application does.

Past the boundary, the application PDP decides what the subject may do, and the ontology does not model it. That is a decision rather than an omission, and it is enforced: an application verb cannot enter the platform action scheme, and an entitlement outside the platform dimensions cannot be evaluated at ingress. The request path ends at /12345, which is an order — the platform never learns that, and must not.

rows: Platform ingress (PEP)
What is this request?
Route bindings, subject identifier, session handle, journey definition — resolution only
Platform PDP
May it cross the boundary?
Membership, the five dimensions, enablement scope, subscription and offering coverage, assurance
Application PDP
What may the subject do?
Roles, business rules, record-level access, limits — application-owned, out of scope

steps.heading: The check that joins the two halves
steps.body:
Before any dimension is evaluated, one thing must hold that is easy to overlook: the principal must be entitled to act for the tenant at all.

The two halves of a request are resolved independently — the route resolves the tenant, the token resolves the principal — and every entitlement grant is held by the tenant, not the principal. So without a membership record, a valid token for anyone would satisfy every tenant-level check at any tenant's address. Membership is the join, and it is deliberately a governed record with a lifecycle and an approver rather than a bare link, because the access-review question is not whether the link exists but when it was granted and by whom.

One principal may hold memberships in several tenants. Consultants, dual-capacity staff and the employee who is also a customer are ordinary cases, not exceptions to design around.

steps.heading: Level 1 — platform entitlements
steps.body:
Five dimensions, and only five. They are members of a closed SKOS scheme, so the set cannot grow by accident: adding a sixth is a deliberate, versioned change to a module that already requires security-architecture review.

Each answers a question ingress can settle without asking the application anything, and each is determinable from evidence the platform controls rather than from anything the caller asserts.

Note how little of this comes from the token. Tenant is resolved from the route's domain and path binding; environment and region from which ingress deployment received the request; channel from the session's device class. The token contributes identity and assurance — not one of the five dimensions is a claim.

steps.heading: Level 2 — application admission
steps.body:
Still enforced by ingress, but defined by the control plane rather than hard-coded. Ingress does not know what any application does; it enforces a generic model — subject, action, target, decision — against governed configuration.

An application is reachable when four things hold together: the tenant owns it, a current approved enablement covers the scope, the owner holds active subscriptions for the application's confirmed capability requirements, and offerings cover that scope. The last one matters because no parity is assumed across regions and environments — a capability exists where an offering says it does.

Underneath all of it sits the route binding: the domain and path that resolved the tenant in the first place. That binding is itself a governed declaration, so the chain from address to admitted request is approvable end to end.

steps.heading: Level 3 — inside the application
steps.body:
Roles, scopes, record-level rules, transactional limits, four-eyes checks on a payment — none of it is modelled here, and that is a decision rather than an omission.

The moment ingress starts interpreting an application's verbs, the small-vocabulary property is gone and every application team acquires a lever on the shared enforcement stack. So the ontology refuses the question: `core:Application` says explicitly that what a subject may do inside is application-owned and out of scope.

steps.heading: How the boundary is enforced, not just described
steps.body:
Two closure invariants keep the line where it is. Both are expected to return nothing, and both have a deliberately broken instance in the negative test corpus — an invariant that cannot demonstrably fire does not count.

The first stops a foreign entitlement dimension being evaluated at ingress. The second stops an application verb reaching a platform decision: an action like "approve payment" typed into the platform action class is caught even though it is structurally valid RDF.

steps.heading: The test to apply to a candidate entitlement
steps.body:
When someone proposes a new coarse-grained entitlement, four questions decide whether it belongs at Level 1:

1. Can ingress determine it without trusting the application or the caller? Region, environment and channel pass; "is this user a supervisor" does not.
2. Is it about crossing a boundary, or about what happens past it? Crossing is Level 1 or 2; anything else is Level 3.
3. Is it stable? The vocabulary's value is that it changes rarely — a dimension that needs new members per product is an application concern.
4. Is it platform-owned? If an application team would maintain its values, it does not belong in the platform scheme.

A proposal that fails any of these is usually an attribute assertion feeding application policy, not a platform dimension.

openQuestions: Do environment and region belong as entitlement dimensions at all, given they are resolved from where the request landed rather than from tenant configuration — or are they properly deployment facts that policy reads, with the grant a redundant assertion? The same question now applies to tenant.access, since tenancy comes from the request URL rather than from anything the tenant presents.

If tenant context comes from host and path, is tenant.access enforcing anything the routing has not already decided? Put sharply: does a request that reaches a tenant's hostname ever fail tenant.access, and if not, is the dimension real or ceremonial — now that membership carries the principal-to-tenant check that actually bites?

Is tenant membership a sixth entitlement dimension, or identity data that sits beside the dimensions? It is currently modelled as governed control-plane state rather than a grant, on the grounds that a grant says what a tenant may do while membership says who may act as it — but the boundary is worth testing.

Application admission currently answers reachability of the application boundary. Do we also need a coarse 'capability class' notion at Level 2 — for example admitting a tenant to a read-only view of an application — or does that immediately become Level 3?

The agent channel is a dimension today, but delegation is deliberately unmodelled. For an agent acting on a human's behalf, is channel.access on the tenant sufficient, or does admission need the delegation chain before we can allow it in production?
Which side of the line does step-up assurance sit on? The AAL guard runs at the platform layer today, but the trigger for step-up is nearly always an application-level action.

explainers.title: Principles at a glance
explainers.subtitle: What a principle is, how one is derived, what each one means, and which candidates were evaluated and why they stand where they do
explainers.audience: Anyone reading or proposing a change to the ontology — architects, reviewers, and agents checking a proposal against the rules.
explainers.summary: A decision picks among alternatives once. A principle constrains every future pick. This ontology keeps twenty, each stated once, each with a test a proposal is checked against, and each tied to the invariants that enforce it. Nothing becomes a principle by being asserted: a candidate is evaluated against four fitness criteria, and most candidates end up recorded as decisions, out of scope, or not yet decided.

steps.heading: What a principle is
steps.body: Three kinds of statement live in this repository and they are kept apart. A definition says what a term denotes. A decision records one choice among alternatives at one point in time, with what was rejected and why. A principle is a rule the ontology obeys: it constrains every future decision, it can be phrased as a test, and something enforces it. The layer exists because one rule, 'the token is evidence, the grant is authority', had been restated in five places and was drifting into five versions. Now each rule is stated once, in principles.json, and referenced everywhere else.

steps.heading: How a principle is derived
steps.body: A candidate sentence is evaluated, never simply added. It passes only if it meets all four criteria: generative — it has already produced more than one decision or invariant; testable — it can be asked as a question of a new proposal; a commitment, not a choice — it constrains all future selections rather than making one; enforced or enforceable — an invariant, build check or CI gate realises it. Candidates that fail are recorded with the reason so the evaluation is not repeated — kept as decisions, out of scope, or terms-first; a few were later promoted once the terms existed, and the record says so. Each row below shows the principle's live status: confirmed once a decision was made because of it, provisional until then. A promoted principle carries its scope (contract, CI, runtime-asserted, review-time), any open exception with an owner and a backlog address, and a status: provisional until some decision is made because of it, confirmed after. Evaluating a candidate has repeatedly found gaps — an undelivered invariant, an optional actor on a decision, a self-approved membership in the seed data — which is the strongest evidence a rule is real.

rows: Generative
Has it already produced more than one decision or invariant? A rule applied once is a decision; a principle keeps producing them.
Testable
Can it be turned into a question a reviewer asks of every new proposal, with a yes or no answer? If it cannot, it is a slogan.
Commitment
Does it constrain every future choice, or make one?
Enforced
Which shape, gate or check rejects a violation? If none, can one be written?

steps.heading: Platform principles — what the platform obeys
steps.body: These constrain the platform's behaviour and are enforced by SHACL shapes over platform data. Where the runtime half cannot be seen in the graph, the principle says so and claims only the contract half.

rows: P1 The boundary, not the resource
The platform decides whether a request may enter an application at a deployment: tenant, environment, region, channel. What it may do inside is the application's decision, never the platform's.
Ingress asks 'may this tenant's subject enter digital-bank at this endpoint in prod-US', never 'may they view account 42'.
Keeps the platform ignorant of application internals, so an application can be replaced by an opaque identifier and every platform check still works.
P2 Governance defines; enforcement actuates
Whatever defines desired state never enforces it, and whatever enforces never defines.
The control plane declares that a route binds tenant T; ingress enforces it and cannot change it.
A component that both decides and enforces its own configuration is the loop an auditor looks for first.
P3 Agents execute; humans authorize

Any automation may act — a scheduled job, a service, an AI agent — whether the platform, a tenant or an external legal entity runs it. Every grant of authority carries a human approval by a member of the party whose authority it is: the tenant's for tenant authority, the platform's for platform authority. Revocation is exempt.

A provisioning agent run by a third party executes a data-plane change under a declaration a platform member approved: allowed. The same agent's admission to a tenant approved by its operator's staff: rejected — they are members of no authorizing party. Withdrawing the agent's access needs no approval at all.

Automation scales action; accountability must not scale away with it — least of all when the automation is somebody else's. Operating an agent and authorizing it are two accountabilities, and the second never follows from the first.
P4 The token is evidence; the grant is authority
A token proves who the caller is. It never says what they may do. What they may do is decided by grants, which can be withdrawn at any time without touching the token.
Alice's token proves it is Alice. Her grants decide what she can actually do. Take her grants away and her next request is denied, even though her token is still valid.
Claims freeze at issuance; entitlements must not.
P12 One path, no bypass
There is one way to reach anything the platform governs, and it is the governed way. Reaching it any other way is a violation, not an exception.

A request reaches an application only through a route with an enforcement point in front of it. A change reaches a data plane only through a declaration. A grant exists only because governance produced it. Anything arriving without that trail is rejected.
Alternate paths are where controls are quietly bypassed.
P13 Decisions are policy-based and externalized
Every decision evaluates a named policy at a named decision point; the enforcement point is a different component.
A decision names its policy, its action, its outcome and its PDP; a node may not be both PDP and PEP.
Decisions embedded in code cannot be audited, changed or reasoned about.
P15 Trust boundaries fail closed
If the platform cannot tell whether a request should be allowed, it says no. Missing or out-of-date information never quietly turns into a yes.

A request arrives and something needed to check it is missing, stale, or the check itself cannot complete. The request is refused and the gap is reported, rather than let through on the assumption it was probably fine.
Security is rarely lost by decision. It is lost when something breaks and traffic keeps flowing. Failing closed turns a broken control into a visible outage instead of a silent hole.
P16 Isolation boundaries are explicit and enforced
Every isolation boundary is stated and every crossing rejected; a declaration's reach is bounded by scope.
A route serving another tenant's application is a cross-tenant endpoint; a cell-per-tenant data plane serving two tenants is a violation.
Blast radius is a design property only if the model can compute it (CQ-8).
P17 Every action is traceable
Every request and security-relevant change leaves evidence tracing to the responsible principal — who acted and who authorized.
A policy change names its executor and its human approver; a decision names its requesting principal; a record whose actor is optional is not evidence.
'Who did this, and who let them' must be answerable after the fact, hop by hop.
P18 Intent precedes state
Nothing exists without a reason upstream. It goes no further than the reason, and ends when the reason ends.
A tenant subscribes to a capability. The platform provisions it for that tenant, only where the subscription covers, and tears it down when the subscription ends.
Every access has a reason, stays inside it, and does not outlive it. That rules out standing access nobody can justify.
P19 No one approves their own act
The executor of a change is never its approver; the principal an admission grants access to never approves it.
alice may not approve her own tenant membership; an agent's change is approved by someone other than the agent.
Separation of duties is the control auditors test first, and it was one shape away from enforced.
P20 Consumers depend on contracts, never on implementations

A capability is consumed through its published contract; a consumer depends on a contract version, never on what realises the capability; a contract changes only through a published, approved version.
An application's requirement pins version 1.2.0 of the managed-database contract; a version published without a change declaration, or a consumer left on a retired version, is a violation.
Consumers survive re-implementation; a change to an interface has an approver and a history.
P21 Data does not cross a jurisdiction without a recorded basis

A tenant's data of each category has jurisdictions it must stay in and may sit in; storing, operating or admitting access to it from any other is a crossing, allowed only under a transfer permission with a basis. Jurisdiction is law, not location.

A tenant's customer data in a US region while its residency requires the EU, a plane operated by an entity under another jurisdiction, or an admission resolved from one — each a violation unless a permission with a basis exists.
Residency and sovereignty become facts the graph defends at provisioning and admission, rather than clauses in a contract nobody can run.

steps.heading: Modelling principles — the form of the ontology
steps.body: These constrain how the model is built and are enforced by OWL axioms and build checks over the ontology itself.

rows: P5 An identifier resolves to an entity; it does not substitute for one
A name in a namespace points at a thing; it is never used in place of the thing.
A domain resolves to a tenant through a governed route binding; the domain is not the tenant. A client_id identifies a registration, nothing more.
Substituting identifiers for entities is how tenancy, sessions and callers get confused with their labels.
P6 OWL for semantics, SHACL for contracts
OWL defines what a term means. SHACL decides what data is accepted. The two are never mixed: a definition never doubles as a validation rule.
OWL says a session is bound to a principal; SHACL says every session must have exactly one expiry.
Meaning and admission rules change at different speeds and answer to different reviewers.
P7 Vocabularies are closed schemes of individuals
A fixed set of values is a SKOS scheme, and membership in it is machine-checked.
Decision outcomes are exactly Permit, Deny, Indeterminate, NotApplicable; a fifth is a violation.
Open string vocabularies drift; closed schemes make 'deliberately small and stable' checkable.
P8 Specifications first, never products
Align to open specifications, then recorded platform decisions, then custom terms; name no products; record every departure.
RFC 9493 subject identifiers and DPoP are named and declared on their terms; an IdP vendor is not. Keeping the session id out of the token is a recorded deviation (D56).
A vocabulary that encodes today's implementation ages badly.
P14 Principals are modelled uniformly
Humans, services and agents share one identity and authorization model; they differ by attributes and permitted flows.
Human and workload are disjoint subclasses of one Principal class; every binding types to the common class; only flows differ, such as approval requiring a human.
Parallel mechanisms per kind of caller are where one kind escapes the controls.

steps.heading: Method principles — how the layer is worked
steps.body: These constrain how the ontology itself is developed and are enforced by CI gates and review-time tests.

rows: P9 Questions before terms
A term exists to answer a competency question; add the question first.
CQ-8, 'which tenants' data planes are reachable from a declaration', existed before its query; zone is not modelled because no question yet needs it.
Scope creep in a vocabulary is permanent; a question is the cheapest gate.
P10 An invariant that cannot demonstrably fire does not count
Every violation-level constraint has a broken instance in the negative corpus, and CI asserts that it fires.
Fifty-two invariants fire on every build; one that stops firing fails the build.
A constraint that has never rejected anything is a hope, not a control.

steps.heading: Evaluated and not promoted, or not yet
steps.body: Every candidate is recorded with its verdict so the argument is not had twice. Most fail one criterion cleanly. Some were valid but out of scope until a module existed, and were promoted once it did — the register keeps the original verdict beside the promotion. One principle was demoted for never generating a decision.

rows: Events are PROV activities (D41); Two clients, kept apart (D47); Decisions name their PDP (D49); No cross-scope parity (D16); One logical management plane (D01)
Five foundational choices
Decisions. Each picks once and constrains nothing beyond itself; each is correctly attributed to the principle it applies.
A definition denotes, nothing else
Definition style
Absorbed into governance prose when P11 was demoted; the fitness criteria apply it at promotion.
Deny by default
No grant, no permit
Undecided. A corollary of P4 plus a combining rule, which is a decision: the policy declares its required dimensions and a permit needs a grant on each. Waits on that decision.
Controls are enforced by the platform, not delegated
Applications do not re-enforce platform controls
Not promoted. A corollary of P1 and P2; its one novel clause cannot be enforced because P1 keeps application internals out of the graph.
Capabilities are consumed through published contracts
Consumers depend on contracts
Promoted as P20 once the contract module existed (D62). Out of scope before that.
Substitutability at the seams that matter
Active substitution of critical dependencies
Not promoted. Out of scope: no infrastructure-dependency concept. Its one in-scope seam, the identity provider, is a backlog question — identifiers are issuer-scoped, so switching is a migration.
Least privilege by default
Minimal access
Not promoted as worded. 'Least' has no baseline of need for principals; 'by default' is the deny-by-default question. Its rule became P18.
Every guarantee is measured
Unmeasured claims are aspirational
Not promoted. At method level it is P10; at platform level it became CommitmentShape in the commitment module.
Non-functionals are scope, not overhead
A capability is not complete until its NFRs hold
Not promoted. A definition of done; becomes the readiness gate once offerings gain an available state.
P11 Every kind of statement has exactly one home
One home per statement
Demoted. A convention no decision ever applied; its rule lives in governance.
Dependency is unidirectional
Applications depend on the platform, never the reverse
Not promoted. A consequence of P1, now stated on it; the two untyped edges that could have broken it were closed (D60).
Data does not cross a jurisdiction without a recorded basis
Residency, sovereignty, access as crossings
Promoted as P21 once the jurisdiction model existed (D63, D64). Terms-first before that.
Performance is a core platform capability
Benchmark features in isolation
Not promoted. An engineering practice; two of its pieces — the kind of evidence behind a measurement, and industry benchmarks as floors — are terms-first.
Nothing is stored without a question
Data minimisation as P9 applied to facts
Promotable now: five decisions embody it and the questions are its baseline of need. Awaiting the go-ahead; retention would be its known exception.

steps.heading: Reading a principle card
steps.body: Each card shows the statement and its test, the shapes that enforce it, the decisions that apply it, and three things beyond the statement: a status — confirmed once a decision was made because of the principle, provisional until then; a scope — which of contract, CI, runtime-asserted and review-time actually hold; and any open exception, with the backlog section that owns the work. Below the cards sits the list of candidates evaluated and not promoted, each with its reason, so that the same argument is not had twice.

openQuestions: Deny by default: whether the absence of any grant is itself a deny remains undecided. P15 settles the absence-of-decision case and P18 the justification case; this is the one left.
Several principles are provisional: they were promoted on decisions made before they were stated. Each is confirmed by the first decision made because of it, and the rows above show which.

explainers.title: Promises the platform can prove
explainers.subtitle: How commitments work, and how the commitment module answers the availability, resiliency and performance questions
explainers.audience: Platform owners, architects and reviewers who need to know what has been promised, where, and whether anyone is measuring it.
explainers.summary: A non-functional requirement becomes a commitment: a promise the platform makes for a capability it offers, with one metric, a target, a window, a measurement source and a validation mechanism. The module holds the promise and the proof that it is measured — never the measurements. A promise nobody measures is rejected, not recorded.

steps.heading: What a commitment is
steps.body: The platform manages capabilities, not the services that realise them, so a commitment attaches to a capability offering. It is a declaration: declared through the management plane, bound to a scope that contains the offering's, approved where that scope requires it, and superseded rather than edited. Example: the notifications capability, offered in production, commits to at least 99.95 percent availability over any 30-day window, measured by the platform metrics feed and validated by CQ-9. A baseline is a floor declared at a scope: every offering beneath it must carry a committed commitment on the floor's metric at least as strong, and cannot be available without one.

steps.heading: Why this belongs in the ontology
steps.body: A promise in a document can be read. A promise in the graph can be joined, checked and cited. Four things a document or a dashboard cannot do:

rows: A promise is a governed fact
It is a declaration: it has a scope, an approver where rigor requires one, and supersession — the same machinery as every other platform intent, not a parallel one (P18, D59)
Questions are joins
'Which tenants are subscribed in a scope whose offering carries no availability promise' crosses subscriptions, offerings and commitments; only a graph answers it, and CI proves it returns rows
A promise can be refused
A spreadsheet accepts any row; the shape rejects a commitment with no measurement source or validation, so an aspiration never gets cited as a guarantee (P15)
It is one home, addressable
Stated once with a stable identifier, referenced by questions, explainers and agents alike — an agent checking a proposal can cite the promise, not paraphrase it (P8, P17)

steps.heading: Measured, or rejected
steps.body: A commitment with no measurement source or no validation reference is a violation at ingestion. A latency promise for the notifications capability with no feed behind it is refused before anyone can cite it. Evidence is an observation: one windowed aggregate per metric per commitment — August, 99.97 percent — never a per-request measurement. An observation of the wrong metric is a violation too.

steps.heading: Floors and targets
steps.body: A floor is a baseline declared at a scope: the least the platform will promise for any offering beneath it. A target is what one offering actually promises, in its commitment. The rule between them is simple: on the floor's metric, a commitment may not be weaker than the floor, judged by the floor's comparator and in the floor's unit, and an available offering must carry a commitment on every floor's metric. The margin is the distance from the floor in the direction that is good: for an at-least floor, target minus floor; for an at-most floor, floor minus target. Zero is on the floor, negative is a violation, unbound means no promise at all. CQ-17 lists every pair, worst first.

rows: Availability at least 99.9 %
30 days
About 43 minutes of downtime a month. Loose enough that every shared capability can meet it; anything tighter is a promise an individual offering makes on top.
Latency p99 at most 300 ms
7 days
A budget consumers can reserve against. The three request-path capabilities together promise 105 ms, leaving roughly two thirds of the budget to applications.
Recovery time at most 60 minutes
per quarter
A standby target in another region taken into service by a routing change. Tighter than this needs active-active deployment, a design decision not yet taken.
Recovery point at most 15 minutes
per quarter
Asynchronous cross-region replication at a short interval. Stateless capabilities promise zero on top of it.

steps.heading: The request-path targets
steps.body: Ingress, the decision point and session management are on every request, so their promises cap what any application can promise. Each carries four committed commitments on the platform observability feed and is available against all four floors. The targets were set by the platform (D71); a changed target is a new declaration superseding the old one, so the history of every promise stays in the graph.

rows: Ingress
50 ms
60 min
On every request, so its availability caps everyone's; the latency covers TLS, tenant resolution and the decision call; stateless, so nothing is lost
Authorization decision

Fails with ingress in practice; the latency allows a membership and grant lookup that is not fully local; grants are re-projected, not lost

steps.heading: How it answers the platform questions
steps.body: The module answers what was promised, where, and with what evidence. The identity and control-plane modules answer who is affected and where things exist. Neither answers whether anything is up right now — that is a dashboard.

rows: Can users depend on the platform being up?
Which offerings carry a committed availability promise per scope, and which none
Which tenants and applications are affected if an offering is unavailable in a scope
How fast can we recover, how much data could we lose?
Recovery-time and recovery-point commitments per offering and region
Which capabilities are offered in only one region — no failover target (CQ-11)
Will regulated traffic stay compliant during failover?
Tenants with a region grant for one region only are refused during failover, never served out of jurisdiction (CQ-10)
How much latency should consumers reserve for the platform?
A latency commitment at a percentile on the platform's own offerings — the target is the budget
The request path is not yet modelled as offerings; that is the next step

steps.heading: What comes next
steps.body: In order: the production floors themselves — the targets are the platform's to decide; a committed commitment per offering per floor, with a real measurement source, which is also the availability review of every production offering; the kind of evidence behind a measurement source; tiers, only if asked for. Out by decision: raw measurements, capacity, vendors.

openQuestions: Which observations exist for the request-path commitments? Their targets are set (D71) and they are available against the production floors; until the platform observability feed reports, CQ-16 shows 'no observation' for each — a promise made and not yet evidenced.

explainers.title: The shape of institutional memory
explainers.subtitle: An ontology, a knowledge graph, a per-question context, and a language model each do one job. Here is what each looks like in our own model, and what is still aspirational.
explainers.audience: Architects and engineers designing AI or agent tooling that has to reason over the platform's documented facts and rules, not just retrieve text about them.
explainers.summary: A model that can quote your documents is not the same as a system with memory. This walkthrough separates four layers, the ontology fixing what terms and relations mean, the graph of facts written in that grammar, the slice of the graph one question needs, and the model that plans and explains.
openQuestions: Does an agent layer belong here as a way to assemble a decision's context on demand from what is already modelled, or as a pipeline that extracts new facts from documents we have not yet turned into graph data, and can either be built before the other exists?

steps.heading: Four layers, one job each
steps.body:
A model that can quote your documents back to you is not the same as a system with memory. Four layers do different jobs, and the usual failure is running all four together as one blur:

```
Ontology            Knowledge graph        Context               Model
what terms and      what we have on       what this one         language,
relations are        file, in that          question needs        planning,
legal to assert       grammar                                     explanation
```

This walkthrough takes each layer against our own request-path model, one at a time, and says plainly which parts exist today and which are still aspirational.

steps.heading: The ontology: fixing what a word denotes
steps.body: Before any fact is written, the ontology fixes what kinds of things exist and which relations between them are legal. Loose usage could call several different things "the client": the kind of client software a session runs on, browser or mobile; the credentialed OAuth registration a session manager holds to obtain tokens, one per audience; and the business client, the customer relationship a principal acts for, which cannot itself authenticate. The model keeps the three apart on purpose.

steps.heading: The knowledge graph: facts written in that grammar
steps.body:
Once the grammar exists, facts about a specific tenant are typed nodes and named edges rather than paragraphs. Ours holds one such tenant, T123, and its digital bank application, and every fact below is what our own test data actually asserts, not an illustration.

A subject reaches that application through a chain, each link a governed record with its own approval:

rows: Membership
Alice is an active member of T123
cp:TenantMembership
Route
t123.apps.examplebank.com/digital-bank is bound to T123 and serves the app
ingress:Route
Ownership
T123 owns the digital bank application
core:ownedBy
Enablement
A current enablement covers the production scope
cp:ApplicationEnablement
Requirement
The application has one confirmed capability requirement
cp:CapabilityRequirement
Subscription
T123 holds an active subscription for that capability
cp:Subscription
Offering
That capability is offered and available in the production scope
cp:CapabilityOffering

steps.heading: The context: what one question needs, not everything on file
steps.body:
The graph can hold far more than any single question needs. Answering one means walking outward from it to exactly the neighbourhood that bears on the answer, and no further.

T123 also holds an entitlement grant on the region dimension, valued US, and nothing else. Suppose, hypothetically, a request for T123 resolved today in a different region — eu-central-1. Nothing about the chain in the previous step changes; one more fact joins it:

```
membership     Alice active in T123          yes
route          bound to T123, serves app     yes
enablement     covers the scope              yes
subscription   capability active             yes
region grant   T123 holds US only            no
               request resolved elsewhere
```

The context for this question is exactly those six facts, not the millions of other facts the graph might hold about other tenants. Assembling that neighbourhood by hand, one competency question at a time, is what we do today; assembling it on demand for a question nobody wrote in advance is not yet built, and is the open question this walkthrough ends on.

steps.heading: Contradictions become a query, not an opinion
steps.body:
Once categories and relations are fixed, checking two facts against each other stops being a paragraph a model writes and becomes a query with a yes or no answer. Five examples, each real and checked in continuous integration against a deliberately broken instance in our negative test data:

- A capability that depends on itself through a chain of other capabilities — dependencies must form a DAG, never a cycle.
- A route reachable at a scope its application's enablement does not cover.
- An offering marked available with no published contract behind the capability it offers.
- Two active memberships for one principal in one tenant, where exactly one is expected.
- An application verb like "approve payment" reaching a platform decision, which is Level-3 and out of scope by definition.

None of these are patterns a model learned to recognize. Each is a structural violation of a relationship the ontology defined in advance.

steps.heading: Answering a question today is a written query, not yet an agent's plan
steps.body: Every competency question we answer is a SPARQL query someone wrote once, checked into the repository, and re-run in continuous integration against the live data, expecting a specific shape of result. That is deliberate and it is also the honest limit of where automation currently stops: nothing today takes an arbitrary question in plain language, decomposes it, and picks or assembles the right query on its own.

rows: CQ-5
For each permit, the full assurance chain from decision to authentication method
cq5-permits-with-assurance-chain.rq
CQ-7
Does this subject's tenant have the right to enter this application at this endpoint
cq7-application-entry-rights.rq
CQ-8

cq8-blast-radius.rq
CQ-9

cq9-commitments-and-evidence.rq
CQ-13

cq13-residency-and-transfers.rq

steps.heading: Where this sits today, without rounding up
steps.body: It is worth being precise about what exists against what a fuller version of this architecture would need.

Fixed classes, relations, and constraints, checked in CI
Yes — eight modules, a hundred shapes
Knowledge graph

Yes, for the test tenants in our seed data

Yes, for seventeen named questions, each a hand-written query

No — every answer today comes from a pre-authored query

explainers.title: Retrieval is not reasoning
explainers.subtitle: Why RAG hits a wall, and how ontologies, knowledge graphs, and context graphs let AI operate over meaning instead of text.
explainers.audience: Anyone building or governing systems that must reason reliably over enterprise documents, not just retrieve them.
explainers.summary: A retrieval system gives an LLM relevant passages. A reasoning system gives it the enterprise's meaning. The gap between the two is where architecture becomes load-bearing: an ontology that fixes what terms denote, a knowledge graph that records facts in that grammar, and a context graph that assembles the neighborhood one question needs. This explainer walks the problem, the three-layer solution, and how the pieces work together.
openQuestions: At what scale does hand-authored vocabulary become unmaintainable, and how do you know when to switch to learned embeddings over fixed types?

steps.heading: Retrieval sounds like reasoning, and isn't
steps.body:
A language model can quote documents back faithfully. It can retrieve passages from thousands of files and cite them. Yet it can still draw a fundamentally wrong conclusion because the documents disagree on what their own terms mean, and nothing in the retrieval path resolves that ambiguity.

A simple case: suppose an LLM reads four sentences about "client", each true:

```
The client sends requests through the web application.
Client configuration belongs to the customer tenant.
The OAuth client is registered with the identity provider.
Client access is restricted by region.
```

Retrieval returns all four, correctly — they all discuss "client". But which client is meant in each sentence? Is access restricted by region for the web client, the OAuth client, or the business client? A retrieval system returns text chunks; it does not resolve what "client" denotes. The LLM has to guess, using statistical association from training data. Where the enterprise's documentation is internally inconsistent — and it usually is — that guess can be confidently wrong.

steps.heading: Shallow RAG: proximity without meaning
steps.body: Traditional retrieval-augmented generation works by proximity: embed a question, search for nearby text chunks, hand those chunks to a language model. The fundamental unit is text, and text chunks sit near each other because of keyword overlap, not because they describe related semantic entities.

steps.heading: Three layers: ontology, graph, context
steps.body:
An ontology is not a glossary. It defines which kinds of things exist, which relations between them are legal, and which combinations are structurally impossible. Before any fact is written into a knowledge graph, the ontology closes off the interpretations that would lead to silent contradictions.

A knowledge graph is not a document store. It records facts as typed nodes and named edges: if the ontology says an Application can be owned by a Tenant, the graph records that specific applications own specific tenants, and the ontology prevents anything else from being asserted under the name "owns".

A context graph is neither of those. It is the slice of the graph one question needs, assembled on demand or in advance. It answers: which facts matter for this particular decision?

steps.heading: The example: typed concepts stop silent errors
steps.body:
Suppose an enterprise calls three unrelated things "client". The ontology names them separately: a device class (web, mobile, api); an OAuth client registration (the credentialed identity a session manager uses); and a business client (the customer a principal acts for, which cannot itself authenticate).

A graph built on those definitions cannot silently collapse them into one. An LLM reasoning over the graph cannot infer "a business client authenticated" because the ontology forbids it — not as a warning, but as a type error. A statement like "Client X obtained a token" resolves unambiguously: Client X must be an OAuth registration, because business clients cannot authenticate. That certainty is not an opinion; it is a structural fact of the ontology.

steps.heading: Contradictions become a query, not an opinion
steps.body:
Once an ontology is fixed, checking whether two facts contradict each other stops being something an LLM reasons about in prose and becomes a yes-or-no query over the graph.

For example: "A capability depends on itself through a chain of other capabilities" is not a style issue or a code smell. It is a structural violation of a constraint the ontology defined in advance — a capability's dependencies must form a directed acyclic graph. The same applies to hundreds of other rules: a principal approving their own action, a data plane in a jurisdiction the residency permits nowhere, an entitlement dimension evaluated at the platform layer that the ontology reserved for applications alone.

None of these are patterns an LLM learned to recognize. Each is a violation of the grammar itself.

steps.heading: Hybrid: vector search + graph search
steps.body:
This does not mean abandoning retrieval. Vector search answers one question well: "What documents discuss this topic?" Graph search answers a different question: "What entities and relationships are involved?" The two complement each other.

A complete reasoning system retrieves both evidence (via vector search) and structure (via graph traversal), assembles the context the question needs, and hands it to the language model for interpretation, planning, and explanation. The LLM is not the knowledge base — it is the reasoning and communication layer over a knowledge base that already enforces consistency.

steps.heading: From one question to a reasoning platform
steps.body:
Enterprise AI maturity progresses through five levels:

**Level 1: LLM alone** — Powerful but probabilistic, with no grounding in organizational truth.

**Level 2: RAG** — Documents retrieved by proximity, giving some context but no semantic structure.

**Level 3: Graph RAG** — Entities and relationships are known, but the vocabulary is fluid or learned from data.

**Level 4: Ontology-driven Graph RAG** — Fixed vocabulary, fixed rules, deterministic validation at the semantic layer. The LLM reasons inside a constrained world.

**Level 5: Agentic reasoning** — The system plans queries, discovers entities, validates constraints, acts on decisions, and updates institutional memory continuously.

Moving through these levels is not about building a bigger model or retrieving more documents. It is about making the enterprise's meaning explicit and machine-checkable.
